newsitem.title: USA: DEERE DOWN ON FOURTH QUARTER OUTLOOK.
newsitem.headline: DEERE DOWN ON FOURTH QUARTER OUTLOOK.

text.p: Shares of Deere & Co fell Tuesday after the company reported surprising losses in its health maintenance organization business in the third quarter of fiscal 1997 that could continue in the fourth quarter.

"The big problem here is that the company announced during the quarter that they had a better than $20 million after-tax loss in their healthcare unit," said Thomas Burns Jr., analyst at Dresdner, Kleinwolt, Benson, adding that the company indicated these losses could continue in the fourth quarter.
Deere shares were down 1-12/16 at 55-3/16 Tuesday.

Other factors, some expected and some unexpected, could also pressure fourth quarter earnings, including a shutdown of the agricultural and construction equipment maker's Mannheim, Germany plant for a month to switch to a new product line, analysts said.

The company will also be seeing larger capital expenses as it starts production in an engine plant in Torreon, Mexico, in the quarter, though those expenses are not above the company's previous plan, the spokeswoman said.

Also, a shift in the timing of sales in the commercial and consumer equipment division means fourth quarter operating profit in that unit will be closer to the $1 million posted in the year-ago fourth quarter than the $45 million reported for the third quarter ended July 31, Marie Ziegler, director of investor relations for Moline, Illinois-based Deere, said. Some analysts added that this should not come as a surprise as the shift has been in place for a year.

But the HMO business, where the company reported a net loss of $21.4 million in the third quarter due to higher claims costs, higher expenses, lower margins and a strengthening of reserves, was the biggest suprise, analysts said.

"I think the concern came in their HMO business, fundamentally," said Lisa Shalett, analyst at Sanford C. Bernstein. She noted that HMO prices are usually negotiated at the beginning of the year, so the larger loss should have been anticipated by the company sooner.
The problems with the healthcare business also bring to light questions of Deere's focus, analysts said.
"I think it brings people around to the whole question of why are they in this business," said J. Blair Brumley, analyst at Dain Bosworth Inc.

But he also noted that overall the third quarter was solid for the company, which reported net income of $252.7 million or $1.00 a share in the quarter compared to $204.4 million or $0.79 a share a year ago.
"Frankly, there aren't a whole of a lot of holes to poke in the quarter," said Brumley, who has a hold rating on the stock.
